sessions.title: Living and Non‑Living Things
indicators: Distinguish between living and non‑living things
Identify characteristics of living things (movement, growth, reproduction, feeding, breathing, sensitivity)
Classify objects in the environment as living or non‑living
Collaborate to sort pictures of things into living and non‑living groups (collaboration)
Use digital tools to create a virtual collection of living and non‑living things (digital literacy)
Think critically about why a car moves but is not alive (critical thinking)
sessions.content:
Living or Not?

Everything around us can be put into two big groups: living things and non‑living things. Living things are alive. Non‑living things are not alive.

1. Characteristics of Living Things

All living things do certain things:

  • Movement: They move by themselves. A dog runs, a bird flies, a plant bends toward light.
  • Growth: They grow and change. A baby becomes a child, a seed becomes a plant.
  • Reproduction: They produce young ones. A cat gives birth to kittens, a mango tree produces fruits with seeds.
  • Feeding (Nutrition): They need food. Animals eat plants or other animals; plants make their own food using sunlight.
  • Breathing (Respiration): They take in air. Fish breathe dissolved air in water, humans breathe air through lungs.
  • Sensitivity: They feel and react to changes around them. You blink when light shines in your eyes, a plant closes its leaves when touched (like the ‘touch‑me‑not’).

Activity 1 – Living things walk
Walk around the school compound. List five living things and five non‑living things you see. Share your list with a partner and check each other's choices. (collaboration)

2. Non‑Living Things

Non‑living things do not show all these characteristics. A stone does not grow or breathe. A bicycle can move but it does not grow, eat or reproduce – it is non‑living.

Critical thinking: Why is a car not alive even though it moves? Discuss with a partner. (critical thinking)

Activity 2 – Sorting game
Collect pictures from old magazines or draw objects. In groups, sort them into a ‘Living’ chart and a ‘Non‑living’ chart. Explain why each belongs there. (collaboration, communication)

Digital corner: Use a tablet or computer to take photos of living and non‑living things around the school. Create a digital poster with labels. (digital literacy)

Exercise 1.1

  1. List four things that tell you a goat is alive.
  2. Name two non‑living things in your classroom.
  3. Is a seed living or non‑living? Give a reason.
  4. Draw a table with two columns: Living and Non‑living. Write three examples in each.

sessions.title: Plants and Animals in the Local Environment
indicators: Identify common plants and animals in the locality
Describe the basic needs of plants (sunlight, water, air) and animals (food, water, shelter)
Explain why plants and animals are important to people
Work in groups to create a collage of local plants and animals (creativity, collaboration)
Use digital camera or tablet to capture images of local plants and animals (digital literacy)
Reflect on the need to care for plants and animals (personal development)
sessions.content:
Our Neighbours – Plants and Animals

In our homes, schools and communities we share our space with many plants and animals. Some we see every day, others are hiding.

1. Common Plants and Animals

Plants: mango tree, coconut palm, banana plant, maize, cassava, hibiscus flower, grass, neem tree.
Animals: goats, chickens, dogs, cats, lizards, butterflies, ants, tilapia (fish).

Activity 1 – Nature walk
Take a walk around the school with a notebook. Draw or write the names of five plants and five animals you see. Back in class, compare your list with a friend. (collaboration)

2. What Plants and Animals Need

Plants need: sunlight (for making food), water, air (carbon dioxide), and soil (for roots and minerals).
Animals need: food (plants or other animals), water, air (oxygen), and shelter (a safe place to live).

Activity 2 – Needs poster
Draw a large plant and a large animal. Around each, draw and label what they need to live and grow. (creativity)

3. Why Are They Important?

Plants give us food, medicine, wood, shade and the air we breathe (oxygen). Animals give us meat, eggs, milk, skin for leather and help farmers plough.

Reflection: How can you help take care of the plants and animals in your community? Write or share one idea. (personal development)

Digital corner: Use a camera (or tablet) to take pictures of different plants and animals. Create a slideshow and describe each. (digital literacy)

Exercise 1.2

  1. Name three plants that give us food.
  2. What three things does a goat need to stay alive?
  3. Why are trees important for the air we breathe?
  4. Draw and label one plant and one animal found near your home.

sessions.title: Materials and Their Properties
indicators: Identify common materials (wood, metal, plastic, glass, paper, fabric)
Describe observable properties of materials (hard/soft, rough/smooth, shiny/dull, bendy/rigid)
Group objects based on the material they are made of
Work in pairs to investigate objects and record properties (collaboration, communication)
Use digital tools to create a materials database (digital literacy)
Suggest why certain materials are chosen for specific uses (critical thinking)
sessions.content:
What Is It Made Of?

Everything we use is made from something. The ‘something’ is called a material. Some things are made from wood, some from metal, some from plastic, glass, paper or fabric.

1. Common Materials

  • Wood: desk, chair, door
  • Metal: spoon, cooking pot, nail
  • Plastic: water bottle, ruler, comb
  • Glass: window, mirror, drinking glass
  • Paper: exercise book, cardboard box
  • Fabric: cloth, school uniform, towel

Activity 1 – Material hunt
Find one object for each material from the list. Touch it, look at it carefully. Write down what material it is made of. (collaboration)

2. Properties of Materials

Properties describe how a material looks, feels and behaves.

  • Hard or Soft: metal is hard, fabric is soft.
  • Rough or Smooth: sandpaper is rough, glass is smooth.
  • Shiny or Dull: polished metal is shiny, rubber is dull.
  • Bendy (flexible) or Rigid (stiff): a plastic ruler can bend, a metal rod is rigid.

Activity 2 – Touch and describe
Put objects in a ‘feely bag’. Without looking, feel an object and describe its properties to a partner: “It is hard and smooth.” Can your partner guess the material? (communication)

Critical thinking: Why are cooking pots made of metal and not plastic? (Metal conducts heat; plastic would melt.)

Digital corner: Use a tablet to create a simple chart with pictures of objects, what material they are made of, and their properties. (digital literacy)

Exercise 1.3

  1. Name the material that a window pane is made of.
  2. Is a stone hard or soft? Rough or smooth?
  3. Write two properties of plastic that make it good for making a water bottle.
  4. List two objects made of wood and two made of metal.

sessions.title: Life Cycle of a Plant
indicators: Describe the stages in the life cycle of a flowering plant (seed, germination, seedling, adult, flower, fruit/seed)
Identify the conditions necessary for germination (water, air, warmth)
Grow a bean or maize seed and observe the stages
Work in groups to monitor and record plant growth over time (collaboration, personal development)
Use digital tools to document plant growth with photos (digital literacy)
Appreciate the importance of seeds in plant reproduction (critical thinking)
sessions.content:
From Seed to Seed – The Plant Life Cycle

A plant goes through different stages in its life. It starts as a tiny seed and grows into a big plant that makes more seeds.

1. Stages of a Flowering Plant

Seed: contains a tiny plant and food.
Germination: the seed swells, cracks open and a small root and shoot appear.
Seedling: a young plant with small leaves.
Adult plant: a fully grown plant with roots, stem, leaves and flowers.
Flower: produces pollen and becomes a fruit containing seeds.
Fruit/Seed dispersal: seeds are spread to grow new plants.

Activity 1 – Plant a seed
Place a bean seed or maize seed in a clear cup with damp cotton wool. Put it near a window. Water lightly each day. Observe and draw what you see every three days. (collaboration – work in small groups)

2. What Seeds Need to Germinate

Seeds need water (to soften the coat and start growth), air (oxygen for energy), and warmth (the right temperature). Sunlight is not needed until the seedling has leaves.

Activity 2 – Compare germination
Set up three cups: one with water and warmth, one with no water (dry), one in a cold place (fridge). Predict what will happen. Check after one week. Discuss results. (critical thinking, collaboration)

Digital corner: Take a photo of your seed each day with a tablet. Create a photo timeline of the germination and growth stages. (digital literacy)

Exercise 2.1

  1. What is germination?
  2. List the stages of a plant’s life cycle in order.
  3. Name three things a seed needs to germinate.
  4. Why is it important for a plant to produce seeds?

sessions.title: Life Cycle of a Butterfly
indicators: Identify the stages in the life cycle of a butterfly (egg, caterpillar, pupa, adult)
Observe (or watch a video of) a butterfly life cycle
Compare the life cycle of a butterfly with that of a plant
Work in pairs to create a life cycle wheel (creativity, collaboration)
Use digital animations to explore life cycles (digital literacy)
Discuss how changes in the environment affect butterflies (critical thinking)
sessions.content:
Amazing Change – The Butterfly Life Cycle

A butterfly goes through a complete change called metamorphosis. It looks very different at each stage.

1. Stages of a Butterfly

Egg: tiny, laid on a leaf.
Caterpillar (larva): hatches from the egg, eats leaves, grows fast and sheds its skin many times.
Pupa (chrysalis): the caterpillar makes a hard case and inside its body changes completely.
Adult butterfly: breaks out of the case, pumps fluid into its wings, and flies off to find a mate and lay eggs.

Activity 1 – Life cycle wheel
Draw a circle divided into four parts. In each part draw and label one stage of the butterfly life cycle. Cut out and spin! (creativity)

2. Comparing Life Cycles

A plant life cycle: seed → germination → seedling → adult → flower → fruit → seed.
A butterfly: egg → caterpillar → pupa → adult → egg.
Both start small, grow, reproduce and start the cycle again. But a butterfly changes body shape completely; a plant just grows larger.

Activity 2 – Venn diagram
Draw two overlapping circles labelled “Plant” and “Butterfly”. Write what is the same in the middle and what is different on the sides. (collaboration)

Digital corner: Watch an animation of the butterfly life cycle on a tablet or computer. Narrate the stages to a partner. (digital literacy)

Critical thinking: What might happen to butterflies if people cut down all the bushes where they lay eggs? Discuss.

Exercise 2.2

  1. What are the four stages of a butterfly’s life cycle?
  2. At which stage does the butterfly do most of its eating?
  3. How is a plant life cycle similar to a butterfly life cycle? How is it different?
  4. Draw and label the life cycle of a butterfly.

sessions.title: The Water Cycle
indicators: Identify the main stages of the water cycle (evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection)
Explain where rain comes from
Conduct a simple experiment to show evaporation and condensation
Work in groups to create a water cycle poster (creativity, collaboration)
Use digital resources to watch the water cycle in action (digital literacy)
Appreciate the importance of water conservation (personal development, cultural identity)
sessions.content:
Water Goes Round and Round – The Water Cycle

The water on Earth is always moving – from the land to the sky and back again. This journey is called the water cycle.

1. The Stages

  • Evaporation: The sun heats water in rivers, lakes and oceans and turns it into water vapour (a gas) that rises into the sky.
  • Condensation: The water vapour cools high up in the sky and changes back into tiny droplets of water, forming clouds.
  • Precipitation: When the droplets become too heavy, they fall as rain, drizzle or hail.
  • Collection: Rainwater flows into streams, rivers, lakes and oceans, and the cycle starts again.

Activity 1 – Make a mini water cycle
Put a small amount of water in a clear bowl. Cover tightly with plastic wrap. Place a small stone in the centre of the wrap so it slopes down. Put the bowl in the sun. After a few hours, look for droplets on the underside of the wrap – that's condensation; some will drip into a cup placed under the stone – that's precipitation. (collaboration)

2. Where Does Rain Come From?

Rain is water that has evaporated from the earth, condensed in clouds and fallen back down. That’s why the water cycle is so important – it refills our rivers and makes plants grow.

Reflection: Think about how water is used in your home. Why is it important not to waste water? List two ways you can save water at school. (personal development, cultural identity)

Digital corner: Watch an educational video of the water cycle. Draw and label your own diagram. (digital literacy)

Exercise 2.3

  1. What happens to water when it evaporates?
  2. How do clouds form?
  3. Name the four stages of the water cycle.
  4. Draw a simple diagram showing the water cycle and label each stage.

sessions.title: The Human Body – External Parts and Senses
indicators: Identify and name major external parts of the human body (head, neck, trunk, limbs, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, skin)
Link each sense organ to its function (sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch)
Explain why our senses are important for safety and learning
Work in pairs to play a senses identification game (collaboration)
Use digital simulations to explore how the senses work (digital literacy)
Reflect on how people with disabilities use other senses (personal development, citizenship)
sessions.content:
My Amazing Body

Our bodies are wonderfully made. We have many parts that help us move, work and understand the world around us.

1. External Parts of the Body

Head: contains the brain, eyes, ears, nose, mouth.
Neck: connects head to the trunk.
Trunk: chest and abdomen.
Limbs: arms (upper limbs) and legs (lower limbs).

Activity 1 – Body part song
Sing “Head, shoulders, knees and toes” and touch each part as you sing. Add more parts: elbow, wrist, ankle, chin. (collaboration)

2. The Five Sense Organs

  • Eyes – sight: see colours, shapes, movement.
  • Ears – hearing: hear sounds, music, warnings.
  • Nose – smell: smell food, smoke, flowers.
  • Tongue – taste: taste sweet, salty, sour, bitter.
  • Skin – touch: feel hot, cold, rough, smooth, pain.

Activity 2 – Senses game
Blindfold a partner. Give them an object (e.g., a bell, an orange). Let them use only one sense at a time: first touch, then smell, then listen. Can they guess the object? (collaboration, communication)

Digital corner: Use an interactive body app to learn more about the senses. (digital literacy)

Critical thinking: How does a blind person ‘see’ with their hands? Discuss the importance of touch and hearing. (personal development, citizenship)

Exercise 3.1

  1. Name the five sense organs and what each does.
  2. Why are our eyes important for crossing the road?
  3. Which sense organ tells you that food is sweet?
  4. Draw the human body and label the head, trunk, arms and legs.

sessions.title: Simple Food Chains
indicators: Explain what a food chain is (shows who eats whom)
Identify producers, consumers (herbivores, carnivores) in a simple food chain
Construct a simple food chain from a given habitat (e.g., grass → grasshopper → frog → snake)
Work in groups to arrange picture cards into food chains (collaboration)
Use digital tools to create food chain diagrams (digital literacy)
Discuss what happens if one part of a food chain is removed (critical thinking)
sessions.content:
Who Eats Whom? – Food Chains

A food chain shows how energy moves from one living thing to another when they eat each other. It always starts with a plant.

1. Parts of a Food Chain

Producer: a plant that makes its own food using sunlight (e.g., grass, maize).
Consumer: an animal that eats other living things. It can be:
– Herbivore: eats only plants (e.g., grasshopper).
– Carnivore: eats other animals (e.g., frog, snake).

Example: Maize → Mouse → Snake → Hawk.
The arrow means ‘is eaten by’. So, maize is eaten by mouse, mouse is eaten by snake, snake is eaten by hawk.

Activity 1 – Make a food chain
In groups, you will get cards with pictures of plants and animals. Arrange them in the right order to show a food chain. Glue them on a strip of paper and draw arrows. (collaboration)

2. What If One Part Is Missing?

If there are no frogs in a pond, there will be too many grasshoppers that eat all the plants. Or, snakes may go hungry. Every part is important.

Activity 2 – Discussion
Talk about this food chain: grass → rabbit → fox. What would happen if all the rabbits died because of disease? (critical thinking)

Digital corner: Use a tablet to draw a food chain with pictures and arrows. Present it to the class. (digital literacy)

Exercise 3.2

  1. What is a producer? Give an example.
  2. Draw a food chain that includes a plant, an insect, a bird and a cat. Use arrows.
  3. Is a cow a herbivore or carnivore? Explain.
  4. Why can’t a food chain start with a lion?

sessions.title: Forces – Push and Pull
indicators: Explain that a force is a push or a pull
Identify everyday actions that involve pushing or pulling
Investigate how a push or pull can make an object move, stop or change direction
Work in groups to experiment with toy cars and forces (collaboration, critical thinking)
Use digital tools to record and share experimental findings (digital literacy)
Discuss how force is important in daily work and play (personal development)
sessions.content:
Push or Pull – What Is a Force?

A force is a push or a pull that makes things move, stop, speed up, slow down or change direction. You use forces all the time without thinking about it.

1. Pushes and Pulls in Everyday Life

  • Push: closing a door, pressing a button, pushing a wheelbarrow, kicking a ball.
  • Pull: opening a drawer, pulling a rope, dragging a chair, lifting a bucket of water.

Activity 1 – Force detectives
Walk around the classroom. Find and list five actions that involve a push and five that involve a pull. Draw one example of each. (collaboration)

2. How Forces Affect Objects

A force can:

  • Make a stationary object move (push a toy car).
  • Make a moving object stop (catch a ball).
  • Change the direction of a moving object (hit a ball with a bat).
  • Change the shape of an object (squeeze a sponge).

Activity 2 – Toy car investigation
Use a toy car and a ramp. Push the car gently, then harder. Measure how far it goes each time. What do you notice? (The harder the push, the farther it moves.) Record your results. (collaboration, critical thinking)

Digital corner: Take a slow‑motion video of a ball being kicked. Watch how the ball changes shape and moves. (digital literacy)

Discussion: When you ride a bicycle, when do you push and when do you pull? (Push the pedals, pull the brakes.) (personal development)

Exercise 4.1

  1. What is a force?
  2. Give two examples each of a push and a pull from everyday life.
  3. What happens to a ball when you push it?
  4. Describe an activity where you use both a push and a pull.

sessions.title: Light and Shadow
indicators: Explain that light travels in straight lines
Describe how shadows are formed when light is blocked by an object
Investigate how changing the distance of an object from a light source affects shadow size
Work in groups to create shadow puppets (creativity, collaboration)
Use digital tools to capture and compare shadow shapes (digital literacy)
Discuss the uses of shadows in everyday life (e.g., telling time with a sundial) (cultural identity)
sessions.content:
Chasing Shadows – Light and Dark

During the day the sun gives us light. When something blocks the light, a shadow is formed.

1. How Light Travels

Light travels in straight lines. It cannot bend around objects. That is why when you stand in the sun, a dark shape (your shadow) appears on the ground opposite the sun.

Activity 1 – Light line
Use a torch and a piece of card with a small hole. Shine the torch in a dark room. You will see the light travels in a straight line. (critical thinking)

2. Shadows

A shadow is made when an opaque object (an object that does not let light through) blocks the light. The shadow has the same shape as the object.

If you move the object closer to the light source, the shadow gets bigger. If you move it farther away, the shadow gets smaller.

Activity 2 – Shadow puppets
In groups, make simple puppets from cardboard. Shine a torch on a wall and act out a short story using shadow puppets. (creativity, collaboration)

Digital corner: Take photos of different shadow shapes made by the same object at different times of the day. Compare them. (digital literacy)

Cultural connection: Long ago, people used the shadow of a stick (sundial) to tell the time. Discuss how this worked. (cultural identity)

Exercise 4.2

  1. How does light travel?
  2. What three things are needed to form a shadow?
  3. Draw a picture showing the sun, a tree and the tree’s shadow.
  4. What happens to the size of a shadow if you move an object closer to the torch?

sessions.title: Sound
indicators: Explain that sound is produced by vibrating objects
Identify sources of sound in the environment (musical instruments, voices, animals, machines)
Demonstrate that sound travels through air, water and solids
Work collaboratively to make simple musical instruments (creativity, collaboration)
Use digital audio recording to capture different sounds (digital literacy)
Discuss the importance of protecting our ears from loud sounds (personal development)
sessions.content:
Listen! – What Is Sound?

Sound is everywhere. We use it to communicate, learn and enjoy music. Sound is made when something vibrates (moves quickly back and forth).

1. How Sound Is Made

Pluck a rubber band – you see it vibrate and hear a sound. Touch your throat while humming – you can feel the vibration.

Sources of sound: musical instruments (drum, guitar), voices, animals (dog barking, bird singing), machines (car engine, fan).

Activity 1 – Vibration detective
Stretch a rubber band around a box. Pluck it and watch it vibrate. Put your fingers gently on the band to stop the vibration – sound stops. (critical thinking)

2. How Sound Travels

Sound needs a medium to travel – air, water or solid. It cannot travel in empty space.

  • In air: you hear your friend talking.
  • In water: if you knock two stones together underwater, you can hear the sound.
  • In solids: put your ear on a table and tap the other end – the sound travels through the wood.

Activity 2 – String telephone
Make a telephone with two paper cups and a long string. Pull the string tight. One person speaks, the other listens. The sound travels along the string. (creativity, collaboration)

Digital corner: Use a phone to record different sounds in the school (bell, singing, drumming). Play them back and let classmates guess the source. (digital literacy)

Personal development: Loud sounds can damage our ears. Discuss ways to protect your hearing (don’t put objects in your ear, avoid very loud music).

Exercise 4.3

  1. How is sound produced?
  2. Name three sources of sound.
  3. Explain why you can hear a train coming by putting your ear on the railway track.
  4. Draw a string telephone and explain how it works.

sessions.title: Heat
indicators: Explain that heat is a form of energy that makes things warm
Identify natural and artificial sources of heat (sun, fire, electric heater, stove)
Describe how heat travels from hotter objects to cooler ones
Work in groups to measure temperature changes (collaboration)
Use a digital thermometer (if available) to measure temperature (digital literacy)
Discuss safety rules for handling hot objects (personal development)
sessions.content:
Feeling the Warmth – Heat

Heat is a form of energy that we can feel. It makes things hot or warm. The sun is our most important source of heat.

1. Sources of Heat

Natural source: the sun (the main source of heat for Earth).
Artificial (man‑made) sources: fire (wood, charcoal, gas), electric heater, stove, candle, light bulb.

Activity 1 – Heat source sort
Sort pictures of heat sources into “Natural” and “Artificial”. (collaboration)

2. How Heat Moves

Heat always moves from a hotter object to a cooler one until they are the same temperature. When you put a metal spoon in hot tea, the spoon becomes warm because heat moves from the tea into the spoon.

Activity 2 – Warm water experiment
Place a small ice cube on a saucer. Pour a little warm water near it. Observe how the ice melts because heat from the water and the air moves into the cold ice. (collaboration, critical thinking)

Digital corner: If your school has a digital thermometer, measure the temperature of water before and after adding ice. Record the change. (digital literacy)

3. Heat Safety

Heat can be dangerous. Never touch a hot pot or flame. Stay away from open fires. Always ask an adult for help when using a stove or lighter.

Discussion: Why should you not run near a cooking fire? What should you do if you accidentally get a small burn? (personal development)

Exercise 4.4

  1. What is heat?
  2. Name one natural source and one artificial source of heat.
  3. Why does a cold spoon become warm when placed in hot tea?
  4. Write two safety rules about heat.

sessions.title: Personal Hygiene
indicators: Explain what personal hygiene means and why it is important
Identify good hygiene practices (bathing, brushing teeth, washing hands, cutting nails, wearing clean clothes)
Demonstrate proper hand‑washing technique
Work in groups to create a hygiene poster for the classroom (creativity, collaboration)
Use digital tools to make a hygiene routine chart (digital literacy)
Reflect on how good hygiene prevents disease (personal development, citizenship)
sessions.content:
Keeping Clean – Personal Hygiene

Personal hygiene means taking care of your body to stay clean and healthy. When you are clean, you feel good and you do not get sick easily.

1. Good Hygiene Practices

  • Take a bath or shower every day.
  • Brush your teeth twice a day (morning and evening).
  • Wash your hands with soap and water after using the toilet and before eating.
  • Keep your fingernails short and clean.
  • Wear clean clothes and underwear.
  • Cover your mouth when you cough or sneeze.

Activity 1 – Hand‑washing demonstration
Practise the correct steps: wet hands, apply soap, rub palms, back of hands, between fingers, under nails, rinse and dry. Sing the “Happy Birthday” song twice to time yourself. (personal development)

2. Why Is Hygiene Important?

Dirty hands can carry germs (tiny living things that cause sickness). When we keep clean, we reduce the spread of diseases like diarrhoea, cholera and COVID‑19.

Activity 2 – Hygiene poster
In groups, create a colourful poster showing at least five hygiene rules. Display it in the classroom or washroom. (creativity, collaboration)

Digital corner: Use a tablet to design a daily hygiene checklist. Print it and tick each task as you do it. (digital literacy)

Exercise 5.1

  1. What is personal hygiene?
  2. List four things you should do every day to stay clean.
  3. Why must you wash your hands before eating?
  4. Draw yourself and label the parts you must clean daily.

sessions.title: Keeping the Environment Clean
indicators: Explain what the environment is (our surroundings)
Identify ways to keep the environment clean (proper waste disposal, sweeping, avoiding littering)
Participate in a school clean‑up activity
Work collaboratively to sort waste into recyclable and non‑recyclable (collaboration)
Use digital tools to document the clean‑up and share results (digital literacy)
Discuss the consequences of a dirty environment on health (critical thinking, citizenship)
sessions.content:
Our Surroundings – The Environment

The environment is everything around us: the air, water, land, plants, animals and buildings. A clean environment keeps us healthy.

1. How to Keep the Environment Clean

  • Put litter in a bin. Do not throw rubbish on the ground.
  • Sweep your classroom and compound regularly.
  • Dispose of waste properly – separate food waste from plastic and paper.
  • Plant trees and flowers to beautify the area.
  • Do not pour dirty water into streets.

Activity 1 – School clean‑up
The whole class will spend 30 minutes cleaning a section of the school. Wear gloves, pick up litter, sweep and put rubbish in labelled bins. Discuss the difference you made. (collaboration, personal development)

2. Sorting Waste

Biodegradable waste: things that can rot and become manure (food scraps, leaves, paper).
Non‑biodegradable waste: things that do not rot easily (plastic bottles, metal cans, glass).

Activity 2 – Waste sorting relay
In teams, run to a pile of mixed clean waste and sort it into two bins: “Biodegradable” and “Non‑biodegradable”. The fastest correct team wins. (collaboration)

Digital corner: Take before and after photos of your clean‑up area. Create a short presentation showing what you did. (digital literacy)

Critical thinking: What happens if we throw plastic bags into gutters? (Blockages cause flooding and mosquitoes breed.)

Exercise 5.2

  1. What is the environment?
  2. Write three things you can do to keep your classroom clean.
  3. Give one example each of biodegradable and non‑biodegradable waste.
  4. Why is it wrong to throw rubbish on the street?

sessions.title: Natural Disasters – Awareness and Safety
indicators: Identify common natural disasters (flood, drought, earthquake, storm)
Describe simple causes and effects of floods and storms
Explain safety measures before, during and after a natural disaster
Work in groups to create a disaster preparedness poster (creativity, collaboration)
Use digital tools to watch educational videos on disaster safety (digital literacy)
Discuss the importance of listening to weather warnings (citizenship, personal development)
sessions.content:
When Nature Shows Its Power – Natural Disasters

A natural disaster is a sudden event caused by nature that can damage homes, crops and even hurt people. In Ghana, we sometimes have floods and strong storms.

1. Types of Natural Disasters

  • Flood: When too much rain falls and water covers the land. It can be caused by choked gutters or heavy rainfall.
  • Storm: Strong winds and heavy rain that can rip off roofs and break trees.
  • Drought: A long period without rain, causing water shortages and dry crops.
  • Earthquake: The ground shakes because of movements deep in the earth (rare in Ghana but important to know about).

Activity 1 – Picture discussion
Look at pictures of floods and storms. Talk about what you see: What caused it? How did it affect people? What could have been done to stay safe? (collaboration, critical thinking)

2. Safety Measures

Before a flood or storm: Listen to weather warnings on radio or TV. Keep away from low‑lying areas. Have an emergency bag ready with food, water and torch.
During: Stay indoors. Do not walk or play in flood water. Turn off electricity if water enters the house.
After: Help clean up. Do not drink flood water. Watch out for fallen electric wires.

Activity 2 – Safety skit
In groups, prepare and act out a short play showing a family preparing for and staying safe during a flood. (creativity, collaboration)

Digital corner: Watch a short educational video about flood safety. Write three things you learned. (digital literacy)

Citizenship: Why is it important to help elderly neighbours during a storm? Discuss. (personal development)

Exercise 5.3

  1. Name two natural disasters that can happen in Ghana.
  2. What causes a flood?
  3. List three things you should do if there is a flood warning.
  4. Draw a poster showing one safety rule during a storm.
